Imaginary Cars

By: Kate Barry | Paid

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We expose the syndicate that scams people into buying cars that don't exist

Unique Selling Point:
We scam the scammers, by pretending to buy a car though an online auction. We then prove that the car, the auction and the dealership don't exist. We chat to the sellers on the phone, we investigate their bank accounts, and ultimately expose the simple scam that has been raking in thousands of rands every day.

Summary:
A Facebook page advertises reliable, affordable cars at an online auction. Because of Covid-19 Lockdown, consumers are more comfortable shopping online and many struggling businesses have been conducting online auctions. The stage is set for a simple scam. You phone the number on the advert to enquire about a car you fancy. The salesman tells you the car is on the auction, but if you pay a small deposit they will set it aside for 21 days. You pay the deposit, and drive out to the dealership in Springs/Heidelberg/Randfontein. But when you get there it's an empty lot.
There is no dealership, no car, no auction. And you have no money!
Photos used in the adverts have been copied from other sites.
The bank accounts of "Global Car Auctioneers" actually belong to other individuals.
None of the names used by the salesmen are their real names.

Further information:
Some of the victims have taken things further and employed private investigators who uncovered several bank accounts and their details.
They have also done deed searches on the empty Lots and believe they belong to members of the syndicate.
Some victims have opened cases at SAPS, but some police stations have refused to open a case.

Extra Budget Items:
As per today's telephone conversation (01 July 2020) we have agreed to do a 3 day shoot, using 2 presenters.

Derek in Johannesburg

Interviews 4 scam victims, 1 online
Interviews owner of legitimate dealership in Heidelberg who has had between 60 and 70 people asking for car auction
Interview Danie Day PI who has looked into some cases
Interview SAPS spokesperson on why they can’t catch this syndicate
Interview Shaun Blomkamp who runs a legitimate Facebook car sales page, has collected literally dozens of fake names & numbers of scamsters who try and sell non-existent cars on his page.
Do all links, some at various sites of non-existent dealerships: Nigel, Heidelberg, Boksburg
Approach Noordrandmotors in Boksburg about their name and address being poached by "North Rand Motors”.

Masa in Cape Town

Interview Wendy Knowler in Stellenbosch
Interview Matthew Smith/Capitec spokesperson in Stellenbosch
Confront Wesley David Martin in Brackenfell

Additional costs would be the 3rd day in CT. Presenter and Crew for an extra day will be covered by CAP.

Script:


IMAGINARY CARS

V/O: Looking for a cheap set of wheels? Then beware of dream deals advertised on Facebook – they could be part of an online car auction scam that’s fleeced hundreds of consumers. First-time buyer Wade wanted to open a small business and had his heart set on this red Chev bakkie he saw advertised by Car Global Auctioneers.

Wade: Generally they go for about a hundred and twenty. They advised that this bakkie would go for round about forty-four thousand. So the guy initially I dealt with his name was Hendrik, and then the manager he went by the name of Peter.

V/O: Hendrik advised him that if he wanted to secure the car and keep it off the auction, he must pay a holding deposit of R10 000.

Hendrik: Now if you pay your holding deposit, I’m saying they will give you 21 days to pay the remaining balance, but if you can’t pay the remaining balance within the period of 21 days, your deposit is fully refundable.

V/O: Another voice note from the so-called manager Peter, explains why Wade couldn’t attend the auction in person.

Peter: Since this Covid-19, so actually the auction already, the people they’ve already booked for an auction. So they’re already fully booked because we take certain numbers of people for auction you see. So I don’t know that’s why I was pushing that if you can manage to secure it before it goes for an auction that was gonna be the best option.

Derek: Did you ask to see the car?

Wade: I definitely asked to see the car. After paying the holding deposit which was R10 000 I asked them when can I actually come through and see the vehicle? They advise that I can come through and see it once we’ve paid the rest. We paid the rest of the funds.

Derek: What address were you given?

Wade: 29 Springs Rd, Nigel.

Derek: And when you got to that address?

Wade: Literally, we’re in the middle of nowhere.

V/O Catherine’s mother thought she’d found the bargain of a lifetime on Facebook- an Isuzu double cab bakkie for just R80 000. After she paid a R10 0000 deposit to Global Car Auctioneers, she asked Catherine’s fiancé to go and inspect the car at their Heidelberg showroom.

Catherine: She tells me they want more money. I said do not pay more money, because this whole thing is a scam. It’s a set-up, you need to go to your bank and cancel it and go report it to the police instead. But they’ve already got my money, and Petrus is halfway to Heidelberg.

Derek: So what did Petrus find there?

Catherine: He found on the corner just an empty workshop.

Derek link: This is 1 Kismet Road in Heidelberg, and if you believe in fate this is where many naïve buyers are being scammed. As you can see it’s just an old workshop. No shiny cars, no salesmen promising to do you a deal. The only magic trick happening here is your money disappearing into thin air.

V/O: To put her mind at rest, Catherine’s mother had actually asked Car Global Auctioneers for their boss’s ID.

Derek: Now they did send your mom an ID?

Catherine: They sent Wesley Martin’s ID.

V/O: We traced Wesley to an address in Cape Town. Masa Kekana paid him a visit.

Masa: Wesley Martin? My name is Masa Kekana, I’m from Carte Blanche.

Wesley: He confirmed the ID was his but knows nothing about any car auctions.

Masa: Is this first that you’ve heard of this?

Wesley: It is, I don’t even know what you’re talking about.

V/O: He says he lost his ID book a few years ago and showed us his new ID with a more recent picture. Other ID’s used by the syndicate belong to Peter Murray and Nick Muller, with Nick bearing a striking resemblance to Peter. These syndicates often commit identity fraud, according to Cape-based consumer journalist Wendy Knowler.

Wendy: It’s a classic 419 scam, just with cars. It’s all fake, phony, fraudulent. There’s nothing real about it, they take photos from wherever they can get them on the net, and what they do is lure you with a wonderful offer. Bottom line – what they’re selling doesn’t exist. That’s the common denominator with all these awful scams.

Masa: What are some of the methods they use to make themselves appear more legitimate?

Wendy: The language they use, the names they give would suggest they’re first language English speakers, but the actual way they use the English language is not; there is a sense of urgency, the cars are in hot demand. The forces are always hurrying you that don’t want to give you a chance to check things out. This is not the bargain of the decade this is you being ripped off massively.

V/O: What’s more, this scam is nationwide and uses different names. Marike from Mpumalanga thought she was buying a Hyundai iX35 from Bank Repo Discovery.

Derek: What were they asking for it?

Marike: R69 000 at first, but then they gave us a R10 000 discount. They have actually provided us with ID documents and the address. They actually have a website that you can view.

V/O: But all the documentation was false, including the invoice, the address, and the website. It was only after she’d made payment that Marike noticed the strange font on the car registration papers.

Marike: I immediately knew that something was wrong. When I tried to call them my number was blocked.

Derek: So how much had you paid in total?

Marike: Forty-nine thousand.

V/O: Byron Mathew found this Golf 6 GTi on Car Global Auctioneers Facebook page.

Byron: I managed to get in contact with Peter. The price of the car is R100 000. You need to pay a deposit amount of R12 000 in order to secure the car. So I pay the R12 000, he sent me the location which was in Springs. There was no car dealership in sight and there’s no Peter on site either.

V/O: We decided to buy our own imaginary car from Car Global Auctioneers. They told us to pay a R9 000 holding deposit for this Toyota Fortuner, and guess who sent Carte Blanche a copy of his ID.

Derek: Peter you're running an online scam you're robbing people of their money in these times.

Peter: I think you're crazy in your mind.

Derek: What is your real name. Peter? What is your name, your real name, Peter?

Peter: It's Peter, Peter, Peter.

Derek: You've got an interesting accent. What part of South Africa do you come from?

Peter: I'm coming from Eastern Cape.

Derek: Eastern Cape, whereabout?

Peter: Why are you asking me so lot of questions?

Derek: Well if you say that you're not robbing people, that you're not a fraudster then let's meet up and chat?

Peter: I’m busy now, I'll call you if I'm not busy, okay? Then we'll meet up okay?

Derek: Because you're too busy scamming people that's why?

Peter: I’m trying to feed my kids, that’s all. I need to support them, I don’t have a job. Come to my dealership.

Derek: Let’s come to your dealership where is it?

Peter: Nigel.

Derek: 29 Springs Road in Nigel?

Peter: That's correct.

Derek: Okay, so we can come and meet you there?

Peter: That's correct.

Derek link: We didn’t pay a deposit to Peter, but can you imagine the shock of arriving here knowing you’ve parted with ten, twenty, fifty thousand Rand?

V/O: The dealership next door belongs to Mohammed Seedat. He is used to fielding questions from victims who’ve lost thousands.

Mohammed: On a constant basis, every day. Every day you will find at least three, four, five people coming in. At least three or four people coming in looking for Global Car Auctioneers.

Marike: They have multiple, I mean over 80 or 100 Facebook pages.

Byron: They are running this massive ring. It’s all linked to one account which is Global Car Auctioneers.

V/O: This fake website is Goldstar Autosales in Potch. Here’s Peter again, but he’s actually a Radiology Professor in South Carolina; this is a Broadway actor, and this is Australian murder victim Justine Diamond. Another non-existent business is North Rand Motors Auctioneers, and it’s here that Byron’s imaginary Golf 6 is still for sale.

Link: We’ve come to 23 North Rand Road in Boksburg to look for cars we’ve seen advertised on their website. Except the website we looked at – North Rand Auctioneers – is a fake website. The syndicate has simply stolen their identity and made it look legitimate.

V/O: Shaun Edwards is the manager of Noordrand Motors.

Shaun: We see I’d say between 5 and 10 people a day that’s being scammed. I had a guy that came with an invoice. He had an invoice with banking details. I’ve never seen a motor business company using Capitec as a bank to deposit money in.

Byron: I paid it into a Capitec savings account.

Catherine: To Capitec.

Marike: The banking details is Capitec banking details.

Wade: I have a list, I have about thirteen Capitec accounts.

V/O: We asked Capitec for an interview, but they referred us to the South African Banking Risk Information Centre.

Nischal: Criminals in this instance chose Capitec as the bank that they would prefer to launder their proceeds through, right? But we have found that all banks are equally susceptible.

V/O: CEO Nischal Mewalall says the organized crime syndicates use legitimate accounts belonging to money mules.

Nischal: The money mule takes this account and allows a syndicate to transact on the account for the syndicate’s purposes, and in return the syndicate typically gives the money mule some form of reward, maybe it could be some money or it could be a gift. We are talking about a billion Rand business, and not a million Rand business.

Derek: But if you’re paying money into Car Global Auctioneers and the account is in the name of the mule, why is accepted?

Nischal: The only thing that is validated is to confirm that the account number to account number is absolutely correct. There is no validation that takes place on the name of the account or not. And that's because the system is not designed like that. The system doesn't pay person to person, it in fact pays account number to account number.

Wendy: Do not buy online. Car dealers, reputable ones, are all over this country, you don’t have to travel too far. I wouldn’t recommend buying on auctions anyway – even if they are genuine auctioneers – because it’s a voetstoots deal. The Consumer Protection Act does not help you. Even if the car actually exists and it’s just a dud, it can end up costing you so much.

I wouldn’t recommend buying on auctions anyway – even if they are genuine auctioneers – because it’s a voetstoots deal. The Consumer Protection Act does not help you. Even if the car actually exists and it’s just a dud, it can end up costing you so much. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): We expose the syndicate that scams people into buying cars that don't exist
metadata.Unique Selling Point: We scam the scammers, by pretending to buy a car though an online auction. We then prove that the car, the auction and the dealership don't exist. We chat to the sellers on the phone, we investigate their bank accounts, and ultimately expose the simple scam that has been raking in thousands of rands every day.
metadata.Summary: A Facebook page advertises reliable, affordable cars at an online auction. Because of Covid-19 Lockdown, consumers are more comfortable shopping online and many struggling businesses have been conducting online auctions. The stage is set for a simple scam. You phone the number on the advert to enquire about a car you fancy. The salesman tells you the car is on the auction, but if you pay a small deposit they will set it aside for 21 days. You pay the deposit, and drive out to the dealership in Springs/Heidelberg/Randfontein. But when you get there it's an empty lot. There is no dealership, no car, no auction. And you have no money! Photos used in the adverts have been copied from other sites. The bank accounts of "Global Car Auctioneers" actually belong to other individuals. None of the names used by the salesmen are their real names.
metadata.Further information: Some of the victims have taken things further and employed private investigators who uncovered several bank accounts and their details. They have also done deed searches on the empty Lots and believe they belong to members of the syndicate. Some victims have opened cases at SAPS, but some police stations have refused to open a case.
